title: Richard Feynman's Tips on AI January 3, 2025
author: Alfred Essa
summary: Alfred Essa opens by admitting the title is a lure: Feynman said nothing about AI, but he did leave advice on learning physics that Essa thinks applies to learning anything. He frames it through a memory of his high school physics teacher, Mr Bunning, who built weeks of lessons toward a single synthesising moment around Newton's laws. The core of the piece is a passage from Feynman's optional review lectures for struggling students, in which Feynman argues that differentiation and algebra must become automatic through rote practice so that errors do not distract from the physics. Essa emphasises Feynman's line that rote practice is the only way to reach that fluency. He closes by asking what Feynman would say about AI in education and answers that there are no shortcuts. It is a short, anecdotal piece, but it makes a clear case for automaticity as a precondition for higher-level understanding.
points: Feynman treats fluent differentiation and algebra as prerequisites for physics, comparable to knowing a multiplication table, so that mistakes in mechanics do not obscure the thinking.
Essa highlights that Feynman says rote practice is the only route to this fluency, a pointed counterweight to the idea that understanding can replace practice.
Mr Bunning's slow build to a single unifying equation shows how a teacher can sequence content so that earlier material is finally synthesised.
Feynman also addressed the emotional side of learning, telling students that being near the bottom of the class does not mean they are not any good.
The implied conclusion for AI in education is that tools cannot substitute for the practice that builds automaticity.
quotes: Everything we have been learning for the past several weeks culminates in this one simple equation. These four symbols govern the Universe. Let me now show you.
Even if you’re one of the last couple of guys in the class, it doesn’t mean you’re not any good.

What we have to do is to learn to differentiate like we know how much is 3 and 5, or how much is 5 times 7, because that kind of work is involved so often that it’s good not to be confounded by it. When you write something down, you should be able to immediately differentiate it without even thinking about it, and without making any mistakes. You’ll find you need to do this operation all the time—not only in physics, but in all the sciences.

Incidentally, the same goes for algebra: there’s a lot of algebra. We are assuming that you can do algebra in your sleep, upside down, without making a mistake. We know it isn’t true, so you should also practice algebra: write yourself a lot of expressions, practice them, and don’t make any errors.
You should be able to do calculations as quickly as possible, and with a minimum of errors. That requires nothing but rote practice—that’s the only way to do it.
